title.narrative: Transforming vegetable Farming as a business

description.narrative: Increase income for smallholder vegetable farmers, particularly women and youth. Increase the uptake of profitable and climate-smart production practices among 11,880 smallholder farmers. Increase the production of year-round, safe-to-eat vegetables. Build the capacity of 22 agro-input dealers and improve access to quality agro-inputs and advice, with an additional 2,400 smallholder farmers benefiting. Improve linkages between farmers and markets. Increase the availability of affordable vegetables for lower-income consumers.

Smallholder vegetable farmers, especially women and youth, are crucial to the agricultural workforce. However, they face significant challenges. By targeting these groups, we can enhance food security, increase agricultural productivity, and promote gender equality and inclusive development.

The EKN funded project “Transforming Vegetable Farming as a Business” aimed to build the capacity of 11,880 smallholder farmers across Bono East, Ahafo, and Bono regions in Ghana to profitably grow and market vegetables by adopting improved seeds and sustainable agricultural practices. This was done through showcasing better yields and solid economic evidence on the benefits of using improved farming practices. The project also intended to improve linkages between farmers and market, increase uptake of profitable and climate smart production practices for smallholders, increase productivity of year round safe-to-eat vegetables and increased income for smallholder vegetable production farmers particularly women and youth. The project, through the Market Linkages Officer, successfully identified 120 buyers in 16 major markets across the three Bono regions. This led to the establishment of vital linkages between farmers and buyers, facilitating a more efficient market system. New seedling systems, covered ground nurseries, seedling trays, or eco-friendly leaf pots were the most adopted techniques by farmers. Farmers are also eager to implement land preparation techniques like raised beds, optimal plant layout, trellising, and mulching, and to select improved vegetable varieties for their agronomic and marketing traits. The project was initially scheduled to run from November 2023 to October 2024, with a target of 11,880 farmers. However, due to unforeseen complexities the outreach was revised to 6,600. To ensure that the desired outcomes were achieved, a no-cost extension was granted from 1 November 2024 to 1 March 2025.

sector.narrative: The project implemented impactful initiatives that significantly benefited farmers. Key highlights included the establishment of demonstration plots in 14 districts by our Technical Field Officers (extension personnel), showcasing innovative vegetable farming techniques. Additionally, comprehensive training programs covered essential topics such as land preparation, pest management, business planning, and more, collectively equipping farmers with the knowledge and skills to boost productivity and capabilities.
